script:
Hello, this is The Portfolio Podcast for QQQ. Thursday — here is your QQQ recap. The portfolio closed down zero point zero five percent on the session. A near-flat finish, but the underlying moves tell a more complicated story.

Jamie Dimon is warning that artificial intelligence capital expenditure fatigue is real, and Wall Street is listening. Hyperscalers are spending tens of billions on data centers, chips, and power infrastructure — with no clear timetable for returns.

No broad macro data was available for Thursday's session. Technology stocks finished mixed, with leadership rotating within the sector rather than lifting it uniformly. The divergence between individual names was sharp, suggesting stock-specific catalysts — not macro forces — drove Thursday's action.

The dominant theme of Thursday's session was artificial intelligence spending fatigue, and it landed squarely on Nvidia. Jamie Dimon's comments, reported Thursday evening, amplified an existing investor anxiety: that hyperscalers are deploying capital at a pace that is compressing margins and straining free cash flows without a visible return timeline. Analysts have been watching this dynamic for several quarters. The concern is not that demand for Nvidia's chips disappears — it is that the pace of data center buildout creates a temporary absorption problem, one that could weigh on forward guidance visibility. For a portfolio carrying Nvidia as its largest single position at seven point six zero percent, this narrative warrants close attention. A shift in hyperscaler tone on earnings calls is the clearest signal to track from here.

Nvidia was down zero point one zero percent on the session. The modest decline belies the significance of the Dimon commentary, which points to structural concerns around artificial intelligence capital expenditure discipline. The story to watch is whether hyperscaler management teams walk back spending language on upcoming calls.

Turning to Apple, up zero point four five percent on the session. A research note highlighted broad demand for iPhone, Mac, and Services in the fiscal third quarter, while flagging rising costs, supply constraints, and policy risks as near-term headwinds. The Services segment remains the key variable for the quarter ahead.

Alphabet was down one point two nine percent on Thursday's session. Separately, a notable development: four of Alphabet's top artificial intelligence researchers departed to found a new company — and Alphabet itself is investing in it. That dynamic raises real questions about talent retention and competitive positioning in the core artificial intelligence race. Alphabet's buyback history provides some floor support, but the talent story is the one analysts will be pressing on.

Micron was down one point three one percent on the session. A Seeking Alpha analysis argued that SK Hynix trades at roughly half of Micron's forward multiple despite holding leadership in high-bandwidth memory. That valuation gap framing is putting pressure on Micron's relative positioning. Separately, Micron recovered most of its intraday losses after Sandisk and Western Digital disappointed on guidance — suggesting the market still views Micron as the cleaner memory story.

Microsoft was up two point five four percent on the session, the strongest performer among the primary holdings. No single headline drove the move, though the broader rotation into software names with clearer artificial intelligence monetization paths appeared to benefit Microsoft. The next catalyst is any update on Azure cloud growth trajectory.

Over at Amazon, down zero point one four percent on the session. The move was effectively flat. Amazon's advertising and cloud segments remain the focus for analysts tracking the next leg of the thesis. No specific news crossed Thursday.

Advanced Micro Devices was up one point five zero percent on the session. The gain came without a discrete catalyst but aligns with renewed investor interest in alternatives to Nvidia within the data center accelerator market. Any update on artificial intelligence chip order pipelines would be the next meaningful signal.

Tesla was down zero point six three percent on Thursday's session. No company-specific news was available. The stock continues to trade on broader sentiment around electric vehicle demand and any commentary from management on delivery cadence. A quiet session, but the position size still warrants monitoring.

Intel was down one point two four percent on the session. The decline adds to a challenging stretch for Intel as it navigates its foundry transition. No specific catalyst Thursday, but the stock remains sensitive to any update on customer wins or fabrication yield progress.

On the secondary side, Sandisk deserves a mention — down six point eight one percent on the session after guidance disappointed investors. That move rippled into memory sector sentiment broadly, which helps explain some of the pressure on Micron Thursday.

Three things to watch in the next forty-eight hours. First, any hyperscaler earnings commentary or capital expenditure guidance updates — directly relevant to Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices. Second, watch for further analyst reactions to the Alphabet researcher departure story, which could generate price target revisions. Third, monitor any Federal Reserve speaker appearances or economic data prints that could shift the rate environment and compress or expand multiples across this technology-heavy portfolio.

This is The Portfolio Podcast for QQQ. We will be back same time the next business day with tomorrow's news. Watch the hyperscaler spending narrative closely — if that conversation accelerates into next week, it has the potential to move the portfolio's largest positions in a meaningful way.
